Patient demographics:
  age: 64
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Jeweler
  trauma_type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
  pcl5: 36

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Shouting: Shouting, Male Presence: Being alone with men, Conflict: Confrontations
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Relaxation: avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous, Thought Monitoring: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
  Memory: Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind., Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
  Negative Appraisals: Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person, Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture

Vignette:
Mateo has been a jeweler for forty years, his hands steady enough to set the smallest of stones. At sixty-four, however, it is not his hands that trouble him, but the world outside his small, quiet shop. The past, for Mateo, does not arrive as a story, but as a series of silent, searing photographs. The first is of his mother’s face, cheekbone already swelling, her eyes wide with a fear he was too young to name. The second is the floral pattern of the wallpaper in their hallway, a detail that became unnaturally sharp and clear in the ensuing silence. The third, and most vivid, is the glint of light on his father’s belt buckle, just before the shouting began again. He remembers these moments with a clarity that defies the five decades that have passed, and each time they surface, a familiar, crushing guilt settles in his chest. He was just a boy, small and hidden behind a doorway, but he has come to believe that his most important role in life was to be a protector, and on that night, he had failed.

This sense of failure has shadowed him, shaping the man he became. He is certain that he is a weak person, a deep conviction that dictates his every interaction. In his shop, the gentle chime of the door signals not a potential customer, but a potential threat. If a man enters alone, Mateo’s body tenses. He finds himself watching the man’s hands, his posture, searching for the slightest sign of aggression. He cannot help but catalogue the potential weapons in the room: the heavy steel block on his workbench, the pointed scribers, the small mallets. Though he knows rationally these are the tools of his trade, a part of his mind sees only their capacity to harm. He tries to keep conversations with male customers brief and transactional, his voice quieter than usual. Even when a customer is friendly, telling him to have a safe day, Mateo finds it impossible to believe it. Safety, for him, is a story other people tell themselves.

Over the years, these fears have built walls around his life. He avoids any form of confrontation. If a supplier sends the wrong grade of silver or a customer disputes a repair cost, Mateo absorbs the loss rather than engage in an argument. The sound of raised voices, even from the street outside, can send a jolt of ice through him. This has had consequences. His ex-wife used to call him passive, unable to understand why he would retreat from any disagreement, large or small. He has also slowly drifted from his community. The boisterous family gatherings of his youth, once a source of comfort, now feel like minefields of potential triggers. The loud talking, the arguments over politics or soccer, the sheer presence of so many men in one space—it all becomes too much. He has lost his connection to the very culture that once defined him, leaving a profound sense of isolation.

At home, there is no respite. Mateo avoids relaxing, believing that to let his guard down is to invite danger. He fills his evenings with small, meticulous tasks, polishing tools or sorting inventory, anything to keep his mind occupied. He tries hard not to think about the trauma, pushing the photographic memories away the moment they flicker into view. But the effort is exhausting. He has become a sentinel over his own thoughts, constantly monitoring them for any sign that he might be "going crazy," a fear that has grown more potent with age. It was after a particularly vivid nightmare last month, one that left him shaking and disoriented in his own bed, that his daughter found him looking pale and exhausted. Her gentle but firm insistence that he talk to someone finally broke through his defenses. Now, sitting in the waiting room, Mateo’s greatest fear is that he will be seen for what he is certain he has become: a weak man who failed when it mattered most. His only hope is that there might be a way to finally put down the weapons he sees everywhere, and to trust that he can be safe in a quiet room.
